subject: general
question:
If the mode of the following data is 160, then what is the value of x?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/fb47155cdad714c7b78d12c89d260ac84135671654355df0806e148ca20d37cf.png]
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Since the **Mode** is 160, it lies at the boundary of the class 140−160 and 160−180.

For the **Mode** to be exactly the upper limit of a class, the frequency of that class (f₁) must equal the frequency of the next class (f₂).

Given the frequency of the class 140−160 is 31 and the frequency of the class 160−180 is x.

Equating the frequencies: f₁ = f₂ ⇒ 31 = x.

**∴ The correct answer is 31.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

**Mode** = 160

**Class Intervals** and **Frequencies**:

100−120: 12 | 120−140: 28 | 140−160: 31 | 160−180: x | 180−200: 25

**Formula Used:**

Mode = l + [ (f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) ] × h

Where: l = lower limit of modal class, f₁ = frequency of modal class, f₀ = frequency of preceding class, f₂ = frequency of succeeding class, h = class width.
